'''Edna Lee Paisano''' (January 1, 1948 – September 3, 2014<ref name="obit">{{cite news |date=September 6, 2014 |title=Edna L. Paisano |url=https://lmtribune.com/obituaries/edna-l-paisano/article_3ccc29f7-5ff7-5cc4-b92b-e60fa31da405.html |access-date=18 October 2020 |work=[[The Lewiston Tribune]]}}</ref>) was a [[Nez Perce people|Nez Perce]] and [[Laguna Pueblo]] demographer and statistician.<ref name=mathbio/> She worked to improve the representation of Indigenous communities in the [[United States Census Bureau|United States census]]. She advocated for accurate representation of the demography of the United States, arguing that without this minority populations would not receive proportional resources. Paisano put this into practice as the first Native American full time employee of the United States Census Bureau. She has been credited with substantially increasing the accuracy of the [[American Indian and Alaska Native]] census category between the 1980 census and the 1990 census.

==Early life and education==
Paisano was born on the [[Nez Perce|Nez Perce Reservation]] in [[Sweetwater, Idaho]] on January 1, 1948.<ref name=obit/><ref name=mathbio>{{cite web |url=http://jimrodslz.org/cultural_math/namathematicians.html |title=Edna Lee Paisano |publisher=Math of the Americas |year=2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402172918/http://jimrodslz.org/cultural_math/namathematicians.html |access-date=18 October 2020|archive-date=2015-04-02 }}</ref> She was one of four children, including an older sister who died in early adulthood.<ref name="Perl 1993" /> Her mother was active in education efforts on the Reservation, and when Edna Paisano was a child, her mother was awarded the Leo Reano Memorial Award from the National Educational Association for that work.<ref name="bu">{{cite web |title=Edna Paisano: Using Statistic to Aid Communities |url=http://www.bu.edu/lernet/pathways/bios.html#ep |access-date=18 October 2020 |publisher=[[Boston University]]}}</ref>

Paisano attended school in [[Lapwai, Idaho]], and spent two years at [[Boise College]].<ref name=mathbio/> She then switched to the [[University of Washington]].<ref name=mathbio/> Paisano spent most of her junior year in hospital with [[rheumatoid arthritis]].<ref name=obit/><ref name="Perl 1993">{{cite book |last1=Perl |first1=Teri |title=Women and numbers: lives of women mathematicians plus discovery activities |date=1993 |publisher=Wide World Publishing/Tetra House |location=San Carlos, Calif |isbn=9780933174870}}</ref> She graduated with a bachelor's degree in 1971.<ref name=obit/> She obtained a master's degree at the University of Washington<ref name=obit/> in social work in 1973, and as part of her graduate work she studied statistics.<ref name=bu/> Paisano had loved mathematics since childhood.<ref name="101 careers in mathematics">{{cite book |author1=Edna Lee Paisano |title=101 careers in mathematics |date=2014 |publisher=Mathematical Association of America |location=Washington, DC |isbn=9781614441168 |pages=192-193 |edition=3rd |chapter=Edna Lee Paisano}}</ref>

==Student activism==
[[File:Daybreak Star 02.jpg|thumb|left|[[Daybreak Star Cultural Center]]]]
During her time at the University of Washington, she worked as part of a successful effort to found an American Indian cultural center in [[Fort Lawton]].<ref name=bu/><ref name="Resource Guide" /><ref name="Seattle Municipal Archives">{{cite web |title=Daybreak Star Indian Cultural Center – CityArchives {{!}} seattle.gov |url=https://www.seattle.gov/cityarchives/exhibits-and-education/online-exhibits/daybreak-star-indian-cultural-center |website=www.seattle.gov |publisher=Seattle Municipal Archives |access-date=22 August 2025}}</ref>

Fort Lawton had not been ceded to the United States government, and when the military base was downsized, a movement of Seattle Indians sought to acquire land in accordance with treaty provisions. During their occupation of the land in 1970, dozens were arrested and briefly imprisoned, including Paisano.<ref name=uvigo>{{cite web |language=es |url=http://igualmat.uvigo.es/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/EdnaPaisano_es.pdf |title=Edna Paisano |author1=Antonia Ferrín Moreiras |author2=Amelia Verdejo |publisher=Universidad de Vigo |access-date=18 October 2020}}</ref> The building of the [[Daybreak Star Cultural Center]] was completed in 1977.<ref name="Reyes 2006">{{cite book |last1=Reyes |first1=Lawney L. |title=Bernie Whitebear: An Urban Indian's Quest for Justice |date=2006 |publisher=University of Arizona Press |location=Tucson |isbn=978-0-8165-2521-8 |edition=1st}}</ref>

==Career==
Paisano's first job in the federal government was working on the federal [[Head Start (program)|Head Start]] program, with Indian tribes nationally.<ref name=obit/><ref name="Perl 1993" /> In June 1976, Paisano moved to the United States Census Bureau, becoming the first Native American to work there fulltime.<ref name="101 careers in mathematics" /> She worked in particular on issues related to the American Indian and Alaska Native census category.<ref>{{cite book |author=Edna Lee Paisano |editor=Andrew Sterrett |title=101 Careers in Mathematics |pages=192–193 |date=September 2014 |doi=10.5948/9781614441168.098}}</ref> There Paisano studied why Native American communities were being dramatically under-counted in the United States census, which caused them to receive disproportionately few government resources and services.<ref name=bu/> Upon arriving at the census bureau, she described realizing "how important it is for American Indians to know demography, computer programming and statistics: first, because there are very few American Indians in these fields; and second, because, the government is always trying to assess things".<ref name=mathbio/>

In her work at the Census Bureau, Paisano identified a systematic undercount of regions where there were very large proportions of Native Americans.<ref name=uvigo/> She attempted to rectify the imbalance using her training in statistics and computer programming, combined with extensive liaison with communities, and a large public information campaign aimed at increasing the number of Native Americans who filled out the census.<ref name="Census Bureau newsletter">{{cite news |title=Broadening our horizons with American Indians and Alaska Natives |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=umn.31951p010931753&seq=8 |access-date=22 August 2025 |work=Census and you : monthly news from the U.S. Bureau of the Census |volume=25 |issue=11 |publisher=U.S. Bureau of the Census |date=Nov 1990}}</ref><ref name=uvigo/> In particular, she developed a questionnaire to estimate the number of Native Americans who may not have been counted in the 1980 census, and she used her training in statistics to suggest improvements to how the US census attempted to count Native communities.<ref name=bu/> Her efforts led to more accurate counts of Native Americans in the United States Census, which was one of the factors likely to have contributed to an increase in the number of people counted in the American Indian and Alaska Native category in the 1990 census compared to the 1980 census.<ref name="1995 Census">{{cite book |last1=U.S. Bureau of the Census |title=Population Profile of the United States: 1995 (Current Population Reports, Series P23–18) |date=1995 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |location=Washington DC |page=50-51 |url=https://www2.census.gov/library/publications/1995/demographics/p23-189.pdf |access-date=22 August 2025}}</ref><ref name=bu/>

In addition to her work with the Racial Statistics Branch in the Population Division of the Census Bureau, Paisano also participated in the Interagency Task Force on American Indian Women.<ref name="Resource Guide">{{cite web |url=https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED213559.pdf |title=Resource Guide of American Indian and Alaska Native Women |author1=Owanah P. Anierson |author2=Sedelta D. Verble |year=1980 |access-date=18 October 2020}}</ref> After 20 years at the Census Bureau, Paisano took a job with the [[Environmental Protection Agency]].<ref name=obit/> After a year, she began serving as principal statistician of the Indian Health Service within the Department of Health and Human Services.<ref name=obit/>

Paisano retired from the federal government in 2011 and returned to Sweetwater. She died on September 3, 2014, in [[Lewiston, Idaho]].<ref name=obit/>

==Selected awards==
*Bronze Medal Award for Superior Federal Service, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1987<ref name=obit/>
*[[Department of Commerce Silver Medal]], 1994<ref name=obit/>
*Distinguished Alumnus Award, University of Washington, 2003<ref name=obit/><ref>{{cite web |year=2009 |title=Help Put a Distinguished Alum in the Spotlight: Call for Nominations! |url=http://www.washington.edu/alumni/partnerships/socialwork/200901/nominate.html |access-date=18 October 2020 |publisher=[[University of Washington]]}}</ref>

*''We the First Americans'', US Census Bureau report, 1993<ref>{{cite news |last1=Paisano |first1=Edna |title=We the...First Americans |url=https://www2.census.gov/library/publications/decennial/1990/we-the-americans/we-05.pdf |access-date=22 August 2025 |work=US Census Bureau|issue=WE-5}}</ref>
*''We the Americans: Pacific Islanders'', US Census Bureau report, 1993<ref>{{cite news |last1=Paisano |first1=Edna |title=We the Americans: Pacific Islanders|url=https://www2.census.gov/library/publications/decennial/1990/we-the-americans/we-04.pdf |access-date=22 August 2025 |work=US Census Bureau|issue=WE-4}}</ref>
*''We the American-Asians'', US Census Bureau report, 1993<ref>{{cite news |last1=Paisano |first1=Edna |title=We the Americans: Asians|url=https://www2.census.gov/library/publications/decennial/1990/we-the-americans/we-03.pdf |access-date=22 August 2025 |work=US Census Bureau|issue=WE-3}}</ref>
